unresolved_added: The Summary says an eighteen-foot antenna produces a ten-mile range, while the displayed 1.41-sqrt(h) relation gives about 5.98 miles.
The representative counts near fifteen and twenty are not tied to a distribution, target ratio, utility parameter, or uncertainty.
The two horizon formulas use different constants without explaining effective-earth-radius or engineering conditions.
The dagger after Simplex has no matching dagger note on the page.
The claim that co-channel regions are about two hundred miles apart is not supported by the frequency-count table alone.
The eighteen-foot height and ten-mile radius are acknowledged as largely arbitrary rather than calibrated.
EchoLink externalizes inter-repeater wireless connectivity and changes the engineering problem.
The surrounding-grid boundary assumption may truncate coverage and bias edge candidates.
The twenty-five-mile same-frequency separation is not derived from the ten-mile radius or an interference model.
The area ratio supplies only a necessary lower bound and no construction for sixteen disks.
The description of the continuous disk-covering problem as simply unsolved and NP-complete needs a precise decision formulation and citation match.
Figure 3 appears to contain nineteen circles in a 3-4-5-4-3 arrangement while the text and caption claim twenty-one.
The hexagonal construction is an asserted feasible bound, not a proof that twenty-one is instance-optimal.
The inverse-fourth power relation is presented too generally; it is a two-ray far-field asymptote under specific conditions.
The uniform population generator is not specified; uniform radius sampling would bias points toward the center.
The spatial process is not classical Barabasi-Albert degree-proportional attachment despite using the name preferential attachment.
No displacement distribution, attachment radius, initial-user count, or random seed is reported.
Program 1 generates only initial users and then jumps to greedy graph coloring and frequency mapping.
Program 1 leaves total_users, r, and connect_chance unused and references undefined G and frequency_set.
The stated two-approximation requires a precise optimum k and applicability proof that the paper does not supply.
The basic O(s^4) derivation hides user count and candidate-evaluation data structures.
The probability that q independent repeaters all fail is p^q for one user, not n p^q; the latter can only resemble an expected count.
If layer utilities start at p, their geometric sum is p/(1-p), not 1/(1-p).
The downtime/utility parameter domain should be 0 <= u < 1 and the target ratio should satisfy 0 < W < 1.
Program 2 stops when current_utility/max_utility is below W, reversing the intended threshold logic.
Program 2 reuses u for downtime and candidate total utility, corrupting the subsequent user-utility update.
The optimized runtime claim lacks a precise update structure, memory cost, and proof.
The noncircular complexity ratio is undefined when min(a)=0 and is stated without derivation.
Greedy coloring does not define vertex order or a failure state when colors exceed available frequencies.
Program 3 colors a geometric conflict graph but does not map colors to legal duplex input/output pairs and guard bands.
Figure 8 is one illustrative realization, not a statistical or optimality validation.
Complete-coverage uniform examples require twenty-eight or thirty-five greedy repeaters, exceeding the separate whole-region bound and revealing heuristic inefficiency.
The experiments report standard deviations but no seeds, confidence intervals, convergence checks, or optimal baselines.
The 1,000-user cells use one hundred runs while the 10,000-user cells use twenty, complicating precision comparison.
Figures 13 and 14 label subplots as Coverage while their captions describe utility ratios.
The claim that twelve colors imply twelve feasible frequencies ignores channel spacing, protection, duplex pairing, and adjacent-channel interference.
The line-of-sight routine's expected constant-time claim lacks a terrain distribution or early-termination argument.
The O(n^5) claim depends on interpreting n as the side length of an n by n grid; the paper's size definition is ambiguous.
The printed terrain-surface offset and sign are not reconciled with the stated distance-from-earth-center axis.
Figure 15 demonstrates terrain generation but provides no mountainous coverage or repeater-count experiment.
The conclusion calls the Section 4 construction optimal even though only a claimed upper bound was presented.
The statement that twenty-one repeaters always suffice is limited to equal ten-mile disks on the flat idealized domain, not terrain line of sight.
The claim of knowing an optimal solution for most population distributions is not supported by the greedy experiments.
The references provide background but no executable code, generated datasets, seeds, or complete reproducibility package.
